problem: IL visual navigation policies fail unpredictably on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Prior work mostly detects failures with external detectors that do not capture the policy's own failure modes, and then just stops or calls a human instead of recovering autonomously.
motivation: Robust long-range navigation needs a policy to detect a failure, recognise its source in the image, and recover on its own. Failure and recovery demonstrations are usually unavailable in offline IL datasets, so failures are approximated as OOD inputs relative to the successful demonstrations.
key_idea: Retrain the IL policy with a Variational Information Bottleneck loss so the KL of the latent serves as an OOD score (thresholded by conformal prediction), use Grad-CAM on that KL score to localise the OOD region, and use the heatmap to drive a simple heuristic recovery policy.
insight: Task-relevant latent structure from VIB, plus KL and Grad-CAM as the measures, matters most. VAE-KL uses the same weights as VAE-Recon but detects and recognises far better, and adding actions (INet/DECISION vs VAE-KL) sharpens recognition toward task-relevant regions. Recognition-informed recovery beats random corrective actions: the informed DECISION variant succeeded in 8/9 detected cases versus 5/9 for the blind variant, and recovered up to 2x faster.
method: VIB-regularised behaviour cloning: retrain the IL policy with a VIB loss (BC term plus beta*KL(q(z|o)||N(0,I))) between the visual encoder and the action decoder, with no architecture change and no extra data.
KL-based OOD score: at inference, KL[q(z|o)||N(0,I)] is the scalar OOD score.

Functional conformal prediction: on held-out calibration trajectories, compute the per-timestep mean score and a band width w as the (1-alpha)-quantile of the max deviation, giving a one-sided time-varying threshold mu_t + w.
Grad-CAM recognition: gradient of the KL score w.r.t. the last conv feature maps of the visual encoder gives a ReLU-weighted heatmap, bilinearly upsampled, in one backward pass.

Heuristic recovery policy: split the heatmap into 3 horizontal bins and mark a bin as OOD if its pixel sum exceeds a threshold. Rotate away from the OOD side (left/right), otherwise backtrack by replaying cached actions in reverse; call get_help after a maximum number of failed recovery attempts.
Two instantiations: InFeR-GNM (image-goal conditioned, CNN + MLP) and InFeR-DEC (DECISION, recurrent, multimodal), plus InFeR-INet for the detection comparison.

setting.backbone: GNM and DECISION (also IntentionNet) retrained with a VIB loss; heuristic recovery policy on top
setting.training_data: DECISION dataset (Ai et al. 2022): 30 hours of teleoperated indoor/outdoor path-following demonstrations; no additional data
setting.observation: RGB images from 3 Realsense D435i cameras covering 140° horizontal FoV (recurrent history for DECISION, goal image for GNM)
setting.action_space: target velocities from the IL policy plus discrete macro-actions {backtrack, rotate_left, rotate_right, get_help}

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark was used. Real-world results are in Table 2 (Det. SR, Han. SR, time per failure type over 10 trials) and detection/recognition ROC curves are only in figures. The Table 2 numbers are not in the required benchmark format, so none are listed.
results: On a real Spot robot, InFeR-GNM and InFeR-DEC detect (Det. SR 0.9-1) and recover from sensor failure, blocked pathways, close-range dynamic obstacles and infeasible goals. For example, InFeR-DEC reaches Han. SR 0.8 on close-range dynamic obstacles versus 0.5 for the uninformed variant. InFeR-DEC completed a 300 m indoor/outdoor route without intervention. On a 180-trajectory test set, InFeR outperforms normalising-flow, RND, autoencoder and VAE-reconstruction baselines on detection and recognition (ROC curves).
limitations: Recovery is a simple heuristic with 3-bin heatmaps and no memory, so spurious heatmap activations can send the robot back into local minima; recognition resolution depends on the encoder's final feature map (GNM is coarser).

Small real-world evaluation (10 trials per failure type), only a handful of hand-designed failure types, and no standard benchmarks; irrecoverable cases such as dead-ends only lead to a human-help call.
